title: 10 Space Facts That Sound Fake (But Are 100% Real)
intro: Ten facts about space that sound completely made up. Every one is real and checked against NASA or a published paper, with the sources in the description. We start with a planet that rains glass, and we finish with the one that breaks most people's brains: a star where one sugar cube weighs a billion tons. Let's go.

segments.heading: A planet where it rains glass sideways
segments.text: There is a planet where it rains glass. Sideways. It's a giant blue world about sixty-three light years from Earth, called HD 189733b. In 2013, the Hubble Space Telescope worked out its colour: a deep cobalt blue, a lot like Earth seen from space. But that blue isn't water. It comes from clouds packed with tiny particles of silicate, the stuff glass is made of. Daytime temperatures reach nearly two thousand degrees Fahrenheit, and winds blow at more than four thousand miles an hour. Scientists think the heat melts those particles into droplets, so when it rains, it rains molten glass, blown sideways by the wind. A full year there lasts just over two days. Beautiful from a distance. Lethal up close.

segments.heading: A day on Venus is longer than its year
segments.text: On Venus, a day is longer than a year. Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin around just once. But it only needs 225 Earth days to travel all the way around the Sun. So if you lived there, your birthday would come around before a single day had finished. And it gets stranger. Venus spins backwards compared to almost every other planet, so the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east. Scientists still aren't completely sure why. The leading idea is a giant collision billions of years ago that flipped the planet or slowed its spin almost to a stop. Imagine a sunrise that takes months.

segments.heading: Saturn would float in water
segments.text: Saturn would float in water. Saturn is enormous, more than nine times wider than Earth. But it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, the two lightest gases there are. Its average density is about 0.7 grams per cubic centimetre, and water is 1.0. So if you could somehow find an ocean big enough, Saturn would bob on the surface like a giant beach ball, rings and all. Every other planet in the solar system would sink straight to the bottom. Of course, there is no bathtub that big, and Saturn would fall apart if you tried. But the numbers are real, and they tell you something: the second biggest planet we have is mostly very light gas.

segments.heading: It rains diamonds on Neptune
segments.text: On Neptune, it rains diamonds. Deep inside Neptune and Uranus, the pressure is millions of times higher than on Earth. That pressure squeezes methane so hard that its carbon atoms lock together into diamond. The diamonds then sink through the planet for thousands of years, like rain falling through a sky of hot, dense ice. For a long time this was just a theory. Then, in 2017, scientists recreated it in a laboratory. They fired powerful lasers at a piece of plastic, creating the same pressure and heat, and watched diamonds form in a fraction of a second. Somewhere out there, right now, it is raining jewels onto a world nobody will ever stand on.

segments.heading: The red planet has blue sunsets
segments.text: On Mars, the sunset is blue. In April 2015, NASA's Curiosity rover filmed the Sun going down over Gale Crater. The sky around the Sun glowed a cool blue, while the rest of the sky turned a dusty orange. That is the exact opposite of Earth. Here, air molecules scatter blue light away in every direction, so by the time the Sun is low, only the reds and oranges are left. On Mars, the air is thin and full of fine dust. That dust lets blue light pass straight through and keeps it close to the Sun, while scattering the red light away. So the red planet has blue sunsets, and the blue planet has red ones. The universe has a sense of humour.

segments.heading: A volcano three times taller than Everest
segments.text: There is a volcano three times taller than Mount Everest, and you could stroll up it. It's called Olympus Mons, and it's on Mars. It rises about 25 kilometres above the plains around it and is about 600 kilometres wide. Drop it on the United States and it would cover all of Arizona. But its slopes are only a few degrees steep. Standing on it, you would think you were on a flat plain, and you couldn't even see the summit. It got so big because Mars has no moving plates. On Earth the crust drifts over hot spots and spreads the lava into island chains. On Mars the lava piled up in one place for billions of years. Weaker gravity helped too. A mountain can grow taller before it sags.

segments.heading: Footprints on the Moon will last millions of years
segments.text: The Apollo astronauts' footprints are still on the Moon, more than fifty years later. And NASA says they will likely stay there for millions of years. On Earth, a footprint on a beach is gone with the next wave. Rain, wind, rivers and plants erase everything eventually. The Moon has no wind, no rain, no rivers and no active volcanoes. Nothing moves the dust once it settles. The only real threat is a direct hit from a meteorite, and that comes down to luck over millions of years. Tiny particles from the Sun will slowly soften the edges, but the prints will outlast every building on Earth. A few steps taken in 1969, still crisp long after we're gone.

segments.heading: Jupiter doesn't orbit the Sun. Not exactly
segments.text: Jupiter doesn't orbit the Sun. Not exactly. Two objects in space don't circle each other. They both circle a shared balance point, their centre of mass. For Earth, that point sits deep inside the Sun, so the Sun barely moves. Jupiter is different. Jupiter has two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined, and its balance point with the Sun lies just above the Sun's surface. So the Sun and Jupiter both swing around a spot in empty space, and the Sun wobbles. That wobble is actually how astronomers find planets around other stars. Watch a distant star shake, and you know something big is tugging on it. Your textbook wasn't lying. It was just rounding off.

segments.heading: The centre of our galaxy might taste like raspberries
segments.text: The centre of our galaxy might taste like raspberries. Near the heart of the Milky Way sits a giant cloud of gas and dust called Sagittarius B2, where new stars are born. In 2009, astronomers pointed a radio telescope at it and found a molecule called ethyl formate inside. Ethyl formate is the chemical that gives raspberries their flavour. It is drifting around in space, about twenty-six thousand light years from the nearest fruit. It forms because simple molecules stick to tiny icy dust grains and get built up, piece by piece, into bigger and bigger ones. The same cloud also holds ethanol, the alcohol in drinks. Raspberries and booze, in the middle of the galaxy. The cosmos has a cocktail bar.

segments.heading: A sugar cube of this star weighs a billion tons
segments.text: And the one that breaks most people's brains. There is a kind of star where a single sugar cube would weigh about a billion tons. It's called a neutron star, and it's what's left behind when a giant star explodes. It packs up to twice the mass of our Sun into a ball the size of a city, about twenty kilometres across. NASA puts it this way: one sugar cube of neutron star material weighs about as much as a mountain. Some of them spin faster than a kitchen blender. The fastest known turns more than forty-three thousand times a minute. It happens because gravity crushes the atoms until protons and electrons merge into neutrons, with no empty space left at all. The densest thing you can see without it being a black hole.

outro: So that's glass rain, diamond rain, a floating planet and a star you could never lift a crumb of. Which one did you refuse to believe at first? Tell me in the comments. There's a new fact here every evening, so the next one is already on its way.
description:
Ten space facts that sound fake but are completely real, from a planet where it rains glass sideways to a star where a single sugar cube weighs a billion tons. Each one is checked against NASA or a published paper; the sources are listed below.
Which one did you refuse to believe at first?
